result: ETHRA/CCAP neurons are necessary and sufficient for Phase I termination and Phase II initiation. Chronic suppression of these neurons blocks Phase II and III execution and extends Phase I duration, while activation terminates Phase I and initiates Phase II, followed by Phase III execution.
evaluation: Claims C49-C58 collectively demonstrate through suppression (C50-C52) and activation (C54-C56) experiments that ETHRA/CCAP neurons control phase transitions. The data from Figure 1 showing behavioral effects of neuronal manipulation with Kir2.1 and dTrpA1 provide strong converging evidence for necessity and sufficiency.

result: CCAP and Bursicon act synergistically to mediate signaling by ETHRA/CCAP neurons. Double mutants lacking both CCAP and Pburs show severe Phase II deficits (70-90% fail head eversion), while single mutants show relatively normal or partially rescued phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C59-C63 demonstrate synergistic hormone action through genetic epistasis analysis. The comparison of single versus double mutant phenotypes (C61-C63) provides strong evidence for synergy, supported by citation to Lahr et al., 2012.

result: Rk and CCAP-R are expressed in almost completely distinct neuronal populations in the CNS at pupal ecdysis. Few neurons co-express both receptors, indicating that Bursicon and CCAP synergy does not result from convergence on common targets.
evaluation: Claims C64-C67 are supported by intersectional labeling data in Figure 2A showing minimal overlap between Rk and CCAP-R expression patterns. The inference that synergy is not due to common targets (C67) logically follows from the anatomical data.

result: Neurons expressing Rk or CCAP-R are both essential for pupal ecdysis, with distinct phenotypes upon suppression. Rk neuron suppression eliminates all movement while CCAP-R neuron suppression produces weak, irregular contractions resembling Phase I.
evaluation: Claims C68-C74 are supported by suppression experiments shown in Figure 2B-C and Video 3. The complete loss of movement with Rk suppression (C70) versus partial activity with CCAP-R suppression (C73) demonstrates distinct functional roles for these populations.

result: Rk-expressing neurons occupy an intermediate position in the circuit hierarchy, as they are not motor neurons (lack VGlut co-expression and muscle projections) and do not highly co-express ETHR isoforms (input layer markers).
evaluation: Claims C75-C78 are supported by intersectional labeling data in Figure 3A showing minimal overlap between Rk and VGlut or ETHR markers. The inference of intermediate circuit position (C78) logically follows from exclusion from input and output layers.

result: ATP-induced activation of Bursicon-expressing neurons produces alternating left-right oscillations in VNC-Rk neurons lasting ~9 minutes with ~15 cycles, resembling the Phase II swinging motor program (~18 bouts, ~17 minutes).
evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by Ca++ imaging data in Figure 3B-C showing ATP-induced oscillatory activity. The correlation between neuronal activity patterns and behavioral motor output (C81-C83) is well-supported by quantitative similarity in duration and cycle number.

result: ETH1 induces phasic Ca++ activity in VNC-Rk neurons that can be divided into three principal phases with durations similar to behavioral ecdysis phases. Baseline activity rises over 10-15 min (Phase 1), peaks for ~20 min (Phase 2), then declines (Phase 3), with superimposed oscillations that change in amplitude and frequency.
evaluation: Claims C85-C92 are supported by Ca++ imaging data in Figure 4A showing ETH1-induced multiphasic activity. The correspondence between neuronal activity phase durations and behavioral phase durations (C92) is supported by quantitative comparison using the PhaseFinder program.

result: Muscle Ca++ activity during pupal ecdysis exhibits a profile similar to VNC-Rk neuron activity, with three principal phases whose onset times closely match those of VNC-Rk activity. Both show a transition period with mixed oscillations between Phases 2 and 3.
evaluation: Claims C93-C98 are supported by muscle Ca++ imaging data in Figure 4B-C showing parallel phase structure. The close temporal correspondence between neuronal and muscle activity (C94) and similar transition periods (C96-C97) provide strong evidence for correlation.

result: Phase 2 activity of VNC-Rk neurons shows left-right alternating oscillations (R=-0.30, p=0.0004) that correlate with Phase II muscle activity (R=-0.27, p=0.0016). Oscillation frequencies (0.02 vs 0.03 Hz) and numbers (23 vs 18) are similar between neurons and muscles.
evaluation: Claims C99-C104 are supported by spatiotemporal analysis in Figure 5 showing anti-correlated bilateral oscillations. Statistical correlation analysis (C100-C101) and quantitative comparison of frequencies and cycle numbers (C102-C103) provide strong evidence that VNC-Rk Phase 2 activity drives Phase II motor output.

result: Phase III muscle activity and late Phase 3 VNC-Rk neuron activity both exhibit bilaterally coincident Ca++ peaks (muscle R=0.57, p<0.0001), contrasting with the anti-phase oscillations of Phase II.
evaluation: Claims C105-C106 are supported by correlation analysis in Figure 5C and 5F showing in-phase bilateral activity during Phase III. The statistical significance (p<0.0001) and contrast with Phase II anti-phase activity provide strong evidence.

result: VNC-Rk neurons comprise a multifunctional central pattern generator with at least two neuron types: those with large baseline changes and those with oscillatory activity. Approximately 10% of ROIs show frequency profiles similar to the global signal, suggesting multifunctional neurons participate in all three behavioral phases.
evaluation: Claims C107-C110 are supported by single-ROI analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing heterogeneous activity patterns. However, the authors acknowledge limitations in z-resolution and note that definitive determination of individual neuron roles requires further work, tempering the strength of this conclusion.

result: Rk-expressing neurons communicate with downstream glutamatergic motor neurons. ATP-induced activation of Rk neurons produces substantial Ca++ increases in VGlut-expressing neurons (95% of which are motor neurons).
evaluation: Claims C111-C114 are supported by ATP/P2X2 activation experiments shown in Figure 5G. The functional connectivity is demonstrated by Ca++ response in glutamatergic neurons upon Rk neuron stimulation, with the motor neuron identity supported by citation to Daniels et al., 2008.

result: CCAP-R-expressing neurons include glutamatergic motor neurons that project axons to body wall muscles and form neuromuscular synapses. Few CCAP-R neurons co-express ETHR isoforms, but a significant complement are glutamatergic.
evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by intersectional labeling and anatomical data in Figure 6A showing CCAP-R/VGlut neurons with axonal projections to muscles. The identification of neuromuscular synapses (arrowheads in Figure 6A') provides strong anatomical evidence.

result: CCAP-R/VGlut motor neurons show multiphasic ETH1-induced Ca++ activity similar to VNC-Rk neurons, with three phases including a transition period and Phase 2 left-right alternations. Phase durations and frequencies are statistically indistinguishable between the two populations.
evaluation: Claims C118-C122 are supported by Ca++ imaging data in Figure 6B-E showing parallel activity patterns. Statistical comparison (C121) demonstrates no significant differences in phase durations or frequencies, supporting tight coupling between CPG and motor neurons (C122).

result: Motor neurons expressing CCAP-R act downstream of CPG neurons expressing the Bursicon receptor Rk. Selective ATP-induced activation of Rk neurons produces large Ca++ responses in CCAP-R VNC neurons.
evaluation: Claims C123-C124 are supported by ATP/P2X2 experiments shown in Figure 6F demonstrating functional connectivity. The directional inference (C124) is supported by the hierarchical organization established through prior anatomical and functional data.

result: ETHRB-expressing neurons are required to initiate Phase I, while non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons are important for maintaining Phase I. Silencing ETHRB neurons eliminates overt Phase I but preserves Phases II and III; silencing non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons shortens Phase I (3.82±2.8 vs 7.42±3.5 min, p=0.0137).
evaluation: Claims C125-C130 are supported by suppression experiments in Figure 7C-D and Videos 8-9. The distinct phenotypes (complete loss vs. shortening of Phase I) demonstrate specific roles for these neuronal populations. However, activation experiments failed to induce Phase I (C130), indicating necessity but not sufficiency.

result: The sites of action of ETH, Bursicon, and CCAP define three hierarchically organized layers of the pupal ecdysis network: input layer (ETHR-expressing), CPG layer (Rk-expressing), and motor output layer (CCAP-R-expressing). Neuromodulators act both within and across these layers.
evaluation: Claims C131-C135 represent the main conclusion synthesizing all experimental findings. The hierarchical organization is supported by anatomical data (receptor expression patterns), functional data (suppression/activation experiments), and connectivity data (ATP/P2X2 experiments). The comprehensive evidence across multiple experimental approaches strongly supports this network architecture.

result: The functional architecture of the ecdysis network can be decoded from patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity, demonstrating that characterizing neuromodulatory connectomes is a valuable strategy for elucidating neural networks.
evaluation: Claims C136-C137 represent the overarching conclusion about methodology. The successful mapping of network architecture through neuromodulatory connectivity (without requiring synaptic connectivity data) provides proof-of-principle for this approach, supported by the comprehensive experimental results.

result: The downstream targets of Bursicon and CCAP are shared components used to generate all three motor rhythms. Rk-expressing neurons are absolutely required for all pupal ecdysis behavior and function as multifunctional CPG neurons subject to modulation by distinct input layer modules.
evaluation: Claims C138-C142 synthesize findings about CPG organization. The requirement for Rk neurons across all phases (C139) is demonstrated by complete loss of movement upon suppression. The CPG role (C140-C141) is supported by suppression effects and centrally-generated activity patterns. The multifunctional nature (C142) is supported by ROI analysis, though the authors note this requires further validation.

result: Direct activation of ETHRA/CCAP neurons induces Phase II-like rhythmic activity in VNC-Rk neurons, consistent with Bursicon secretion shifting the mode of activity of the VNC-Rk CPG.
evaluation: Claims C143-C144 are supported by ATP/P2X2 activation experiments. The observation of Phase II-like activity (C143) is demonstrated experimentally, and the mechanistic interpretation involving Bursicon-mediated CPG mode switching (C144) is a reasonable inference consistent with neuromodulatory control principles.

result: The mixed activity patterns defining the transition from Phase II to Phase III represent a period of bistability in which CPG modes transiently alternate, possibly as Bursicon and/or co-released neuromodulator concentrations fall.
evaluation: Claim C146 provides a mechanistic interpretation of the transition period observed in both neuronal and muscle Ca++ data. The bistability interpretation is consistent with the mixed oscillation patterns documented in Figures 4-5 and is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2006, though direct measurement of neuromodulator concentrations is not provided.

result: ETHRB-expressing neurons initiate Phase I, possibly by responding to rising ETH titers earlier than ETHRA neurons due to ETHRB's higher affinity for ETH peptides. Non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons maintain Phase I.
evaluation: Claims C147-C148 are supported by suppression experiments in Figure 7. The mechanistic explanation based on receptor affinity differences (C149-C150) is supported by citations to Iversen et al., 2002 and Park et al., 2003b, providing a plausible molecular basis for the observed functional differences.

result: The motor output of the pupal ecdysis network is mediated by CCAP-R-expressing neurons. CCAP acts on motor neurons to render pupal ecdysis more robust, and is co-released with Bursicon from ETHRA/CCAP neurons, suggesting feedforward signaling.
evaluation: Claims C151-C153 are supported by anatomical identification of CCAP-R motor neurons (Figure 6A) and functional data showing their requirement for ecdysis. The feedforward signaling interpretation (C152-C153) is a reasonable inference from the co-release of CCAP and Bursicon acting on different layers, though direct demonstration of feedforward effects is not provided.

result: The architecture of the pupal ecdysis network is similar to other motor circuits governing locomotion, feeding, and breathing, where higher order neurons modulate core CPG activity to generate varied motor patterns.
evaluation: Claim C154 places the findings in broader context through comparison to other motor systems. The comparison is supported by citations to Feldman et al., 2013; Mullins et al., 2011; Nusbaum et al., 2001, demonstrating that the hierarchical organization observed here is a common motif in motor control.

result: Neuromodulator action in the ecdysis circuit has broad scope: ETH acts throughout the input layer, Bursicon regulates the CPG, and CCAP acts on motor neurons. Bursicon and CCAP signal from the input layer to provide coherence by acting within and across hierarchical layers, consistent with a generalized organizational role for neuromodulatory systems.
evaluation: Claims C155-C159 synthesize findings about neuromodulatory organization. The broad scope of action (C155-C157) is demonstrated by the expression patterns and functional requirements. The organizational logic (C158) is a reasonable inference from the data, and the generalization to neuromodulatory systems (C159) is supported by citation to Marder, 2012.

result: Mapping the pupal ecdysis network without synaptic connectivity data demonstrates that patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity may complement synaptic maps to render them interpretable, particularly for multifunctional networks. When critical neuromodulator systems are known, neuromodulatory connections deliver substantial insight into network organization.
evaluation: Claims C160-C164 present the methodological implications. The successful network mapping without synaptic data (C160) is demonstrated by the study. The hypothesis that neuromodulatory connectivity complements synaptic maps (C163) is supported by citations to Bargmann and Marder, 2013; Brezina, 2010; Marder, 2012, and the current findings provide empirical support for this approach.

result: Neural networks are typically defined by synaptic connectivity, yet synaptic wiring diagrams often provide limited insight into network function, partly due to the importance of non-synaptic neuromodulatory communication that can dynamically reconfigure circuit activity.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 establish the conceptual framework and motivation for the study. These are well-established principles in neuroscience supported by general knowledge and the broader literature, setting up the rationale for focusing on neuromodulatory connectivity.

result: The pupal ecdysis sequence in Drosophila is governed by serial release of factors (ETH, EH, CCAP, Bursicon) that act as both hormones and neuromodulators. The neuronal targets of these factors define hierarchically organized network layers (input, CPG, motor output), and mapping neuromodulatory connections defines the functional architecture.
evaluation: Claims C5-C9 present the abstract/introduction summary of the study's approach and main findings. These claims are supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, representing the study's central thesis validated by the results.

result: Neuromodulators act at virtually all levels of sensorimotor processing to tune neuronal properties, profoundly influencing circuit function. They may coordinate activity in broadly distributed circuits over long timescales and distances, suggesting that identifying sites of neuromodulator action is a productive strategy for mapping critical circuits.
evaluation: Claims C10-C15 establish the theoretical background from prior literature. These are well-supported by citations to Marder, 2012; Nadim and Bucher, 2014; van den Pol, 2012; Bargmann, 2012; and others. The methodological hypothesis (C15) is tested and validated by the current study.

result: Historical observations showed that brain-derived hormones and biogenic amines induce complex motor programs, including moth emergence, egg-laying, and postural changes. Octopamine acts as an insect locomotor activator and modulates muscle metabolism and visual processing during flight.
evaluation: Claims C16-C20 provide historical context supported by citations to classic studies (Harris-Warrick, 1988; Truman and Riddiford, 1970; Kupfermann, 1967; Livingstone et al., 1980; Libersat and Pflueger, 2004; Suver et al., 2012). These establish precedent for the neuromodulator mapping approach.

result: The crustacean stomatogastric ganglion contains two CPGs (pyloric and gastric mill) that are reconfigured by neuromodulators. Proctolin and CabTRP, co-released from MCN1, activate the same current but have different effects because they target distinct cells within the CPGs, coordinating changes in functionally related circuits.
evaluation: Claims C21-C29 describe the STG system as a precedent for neuromodulatory circuit organization. All claims are supported by citations to Marder and Bucher, 2007; Blitz et al., 1999; Swensen and Marder, 2000; Wood et al., 2000; Beenhakker and Nusbaum, 2004; Blitz et al., 2004, establishing the conceptual framework for the current study.

result: Cross-species differences in striatal vasopressin receptor expression in vole species correlate with and cause monogamous versus polygamous mating predispositions. Variations in neuromodulator receptor expression during speciation have been proposed as a major driver of behavioral evolution.
evaluation: Claims C30-C32 provide examples of neuromodulator receptor expression influencing behavior, supported by citations to Hammock and Young, 2005; Young et al., 1997; Katz and Lillvis, 2014. These establish the broader significance of mapping neuromodulator receptor expression patterns.

result: Conserved neuromodulators like oxytocin and NPY regulate distinct circuits promoting specific behaviors (social recognition, pup retrieval, social learning, feeding) across multiple species, demonstrating that neuromodulators coordinate activity in broadly distributed circuits.
evaluation: Claims C33-C36 provide contemporary examples of neuromodulatory circuit organization, supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2001; Marlin et al., 2015; Choe et al., 2015; Taghert and Nitabach, 2012. These establish the relevance and generality of the neuromodulatory mapping approach.

result: Molting in insects is accomplished by an ecdysis sequence initiated by ETH release, which facilitates secretion of EH, CCAP, and Bursicon. In Drosophila pupal ecdysis, three behavioral phases are characterized by distinct motor rhythms, with Phase II specifically dependent on CCAP and Bursicon from ETH-targeted neurons.
evaluation: Claims C37-C46 establish the biological system being studied, supported by citations to White and Ewer, 2014; Diao et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2006; Mena et al., 2016; Lahr et al., 2012. These provide essential background on the ecdysis system and prior knowledge about its hormonal control.

result: A subset of CCAP-expressing neurons (ETHRA/CCAP neurons) expresses ETHRA and is required for head eversion during Phase II of pupal ecdysis.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 cite prior work from the same laboratory (Diao et al., 2016) establishing the ETHRA/CCAP neuron population. This provides the starting point for the current investigation into downstream targets.

result: CCAP- and Bursicon-expressing neurons are known to express additional neuropeptides including Myoinhibitory Peptides and Allatostatin C, which likely also play roles in regulating ecdysis phases.
evaluation: Claim C145 acknowledges additional complexity in the system based on established knowledge about neuropeptide co-expression. This is a reasonable caveat noting that the study focuses on CCAP and Bursicon but other co-released factors may contribute.
